title: Sovereign Website: the market around it
about: Data for cartographer.d to draw (carto-map/1) and strategy.d to place on evolution. Positions are NOT given here: this file holds who offers what, with sources. Every fact has its URL and the date it was read; rows flagged in the facts must be re-read. Our own offer: jobs/2026-11-22-sovereign-website/01b-our-offer-relayed.md.

findings.text: None of the five hosted European builders read (Infomaniak, saldiaBuild, IONOS, Jimdo, Hostinger) documents an export or move-out path on the pages read; Framer's terms describe none and only advise customers to archive their own content. This is the nearest rival evidence for our test 'you can move it'. Reading limited to the pages read: absence on a page is not proof of absence in the product.

Open-source static engines (Hugo, Jekyll, Eleventy, Astro, Zola) give the owner plain files and a permissive or open licence for free, but ask for a terminal and Node or Ruby; our offer is the same output made by agents for a non-technical owner.

Open-source AI builders exist (bolt.diy, Dyad, tinykit, Totalum's AI App Builder Open) but all ask for developer setup and a model key of your own; one hosts the output itself (Totalum) and one keeps part of its code under a fair-source licence (Dyad). Nobody read offers an owner-ready, agent-built, movable small-business site.

Hostinger's own privacy policy (via a search summary) says some servers are outside the EU and EEA and that AI Builder sites sit on a CDN with fixed location; yet it is listed as an EU builder in third-party roundups. Sovereignty claims in this ring are not uniform and need the buyer's own check.

Hosted builders charge by subscription (examples read: Hostinger from $1.99 a month on a 48-month term renewing at $10.99; IONOS Starter $6 then $14 a month; Framer $10 to $30 a month; Ghost(Pro) $18 a month yearly). Our published line is one-off (500 anchor, 250 standing as relayed, 50 launch offer proposed): one-off against monthly is the difference to test, not a price comparison on its own.

Of the mass-market and AI-native builders, none read states an export tool for the site on the pages read (Wix, Squarespace, Lovable, Bolt, Durable, 10Web); v0 advertises GitHub sync on its free plan and 10Web lists SFTP/SSH, which are partial answers. Webflow, the builder best known for code export, could not be read at all and must be re-scouted before any claim is made about it.

Several terms keep a broad licence over the customer's content: Squarespace takes a perpetual, irrevocable licence to use, host and distribute it, and Lovable a perpetual licence including for training AI models (with an opt-out for future use). This sits against our test 'you set the terms'. Read as terms, not legal advice.

Where it lives is rarely stated by the builders (Wix, Squarespace, Bolt, v0, Durable name no region; Lovable says it does not guarantee one), while the hosting layer varies: Hetzner (German, Nuremberg) and OVHcloud (French; cites SecNumCloud and other standards) state a home; Cloudflare offers regional controls but is US-based per its own transfer mechanism; Netlify is a California company. OVHcloud and Cloudflare each say something about foreign-law exposure only in part. Our plan makes no legal or certification claim on sovereignty; the buyer's own check applies.

Free static hosts are not equal for a business site: GitHub Pages says it is not meant to run an online business or e-commerce (and sets soft limits of 1 GB and 100 GB a month); Netlify's free plan says commercial use is allowed within its monthly credits; Cloudflare Pages states per-site file and build limits. Hetzner starts at EUR 1.60 a month excluding VAT with domains extra. This decides what 'run it anywhere' costs the owner.
